To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) cervical pregnancy is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening variety of ectopic pregnancy that is often misdiagnosed; (2) it may be related to prior uterine scarring; (3) early diagnosis by ultrasonography is essential; (4) systemic methotrexatetreatment is effective in selected cases; (5) surgical intervention is indicated in cases of haemodynamic instability or failure of medical management; (6) the prognosis is good in most cases;
the most effective treatment for cervical pregnancy is surgical evacuation of the products of conception with or without cervical cerclage.
the most important factor for the successful treatment of a cervical pregnancy is the early diagnosis of the condition.

the treatment of cervical pregnancy and the role that ultrasound plays in the diagnosis and management of this condition.
the management of cervical pregnancy and the role of ultrasound in early diagnosis.
the diagnosis of cervical pregnancy and management options.

there is no single best treatment for cervical pregnancy.
the management of cervical pregnancy should be individualised and based on the clinical state of each patient.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the management of cervical pregnancy is challenging, and the outcome of this condition depends on the experience and expertise of the medical and surgical teams.
cervical pregnancy should be suspected in any woman presenting with pain, bleeding and amenorrhoea.
the treatment of choice for cervical pregnancies is total abdominal hysterectomy, especially when the patient has a previous history of curettage or previous uterine surgery.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cervical pregnancy is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition that requires early diagnosis, prompt intervention and close monitoring to reduce morbidity and mortality.
